E1.name: Claiming a term has been undone using the wrong inverse
E1.example: x + 5 = 12 → x = 17. Subtract 5 to isolate x, giving 7. Simply adding 5 to both sides and retaining all terms is valid, even if inefficient.

E2.name: Breaking equality by changing only one side or applying different operations
E2.example: Subtract 5 on the left but add 5 on the right of 3x + 5 = 20. Apply the same operation to both sides.

E3.name: Treating a coefficient as an added number
E3.example: 4x = 28 → x = 24. Four multiplies x; divide both sides by 4 to obtain 7.

E4.name: Dividing only some terms on a side

E5.name: Expanding brackets incompletely or mishandling a sign within them
E5.example: 3(x + 4) → 3x + 4, or 2(x − 3) → 2x + 6. Correct expansions are 3x + 12 and 2x − 6; use one clearly identified fault per authored example.

E6.name: Combining unlike terms or losing the variable when collecting like terms

E7.name: Arithmetic/sign slip within an otherwise valid balancing step
E7.example: For 3x + 5 = 20, correctly choose −5 on both sides but evaluate 20 − 5 as 25. The choice is valid; the calculation should give 3x = 15.

E8.name: Checking against the wrong equation or substituting incorrectly
E8.example: Checking x = 7 in 4x + 3 = 31 as 4 + 7 + 3. Substitute into the original equation: 4 × 7 + 3 = 31, evaluating both sides.
